name: Alfonso IX of León

title: King of León and Galicia

summary: Last king of an independent León, who in 1188 summoned elected townsmen to sit with the bishops and magnates of his curia — the assembly UNESCO registered in 2013 as the oldest documentary evidence of the European parliamentary system — and whose death in 1230 united León with Castile for good.
details: Alfonso IX spent forty-two years quarrelling with Castile and Portugal, was excommunicated over two marriages annulled for consanguinity, and sat out Las Navas de Tolosa. He also took Cáceres, Mérida and Badajoz in his last two years, founded the schools that became the University of Salamanca, and left his kingdom to the son who already held Castile.

birth.note: Son of Ferdinand II of León and his first wife Urraca of Portugal, a daughter of Afonso I; the marriage had itself been annulled for consanguinity, which shadowed his own legitimacy.

death.circumstance: He died in Galicia while travelling on pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela, and was buried in the cathedral there beside his father Ferdinand II. Within three months his daughters had renounced their claims and León passed to his son Ferdinand III.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Alfonso IX ruled León and Galicia from 1188 to 1230 and was the last king of León as a separate crown. He came to the throne at sixteen, into a kingdom squeezed between a far stronger Castile and an aggressive Portugal, and he defended it for four decades by every means available — war, marriage, alliance with the Almohads, and an appeal to his own subjects that turned out to matter more than any of them.

Within weeks of his accession he held a curia at San Isidoro in León and admitted elected representatives of the towns to sit with the bishops and the nobles. The decrees issued there were inscribed by UNESCO in 2013 as "the oldest documentary manifestation of the European parliamentary system". His reign ended in the conquest of Extremadura and in a succession crisis settled by his former wife, whose son took both crowns.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: He was born at Zamora on 15 August 1171, the son of Ferdinand II of León and Urraca of Portugal. His parents’ marriage was annulled for consanguinity while he was a child, which left a permanent question mark over his standing and gave his opponents something to use. His father remarried, and when Ferdinand II died in January 1188 his widow, Urraca López de Haro, worked to put her own son on the throne instead.

Alfonso was sixteen when he took the crown on 22 January 1188, with that challenge inside his own household and a cousin in Castile, Alfonso VIII, who regarded León as a client. The pressure from both directions at once explains what he did next: a young king with a contested title needed supporters, and the richest untapped source of them was the towns.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: The most important thing to know about the sources for Alfonso IX is who paid for them. Lucas de Tuy was a canon of San Isidoro de León — the king’s own royal church, where the curia of 1188 met — and he wrote the Chronicon mundi in 1236 at the commission of Queen Berengaria of Castile, who was Alfonso’s second wife until the papacy separated them, and the mother of the son who inherited his kingdom. Lucas is therefore Leonese by loyalty and Castilian by patronage, writing six years after the king’s death for the woman whose negotiations had just delivered León to Castile. He is warm about Alfonso and warmer about the union of the crowns, and the two enthusiasms are not easily separated.

The hostile witnesses are the popes. Celestine III and then Innocent III pursued him through two marriages within the prohibited degrees, and their letters describe a king who defied interdict and excommunication for years rather than give up a queen and an alliance. The same correspondence condemns his truce with the Almohads, made in 1191 and used again after the Castilian disaster at the Battle of Alarcos in 1195 — behaviour that looked, from Rome, like a Christian king arming the enemy against his own cousin. His absence from the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, the great combined victory of the peninsula, hardened that reputation into something like a byword.

Read from León rather than from Rome or Castile, the same actions are a small kingdom’s foreign policy. Alfonso VIII had knighted him at Carrión in 1188 in a ceremony that implied homage, and had seized Leonese towns; a king who could not match Castile in the field kept his independence by refusing to be absorbed into Castile’s wars. What the record shows consistently is stubbornness rather than caprice: the same man who would not abandon an uncanonical marriage for a pope spent his last two years taking fortresses in Extremadura that no Leonese king had held, and died on the road to Compostela.

contentSections.title: The curia of León, 1188
paragraphs: In the spring of 1188, probably in April, Alfonso summoned a full curia to the cloister of San Isidoro in León. The novelty was not the assembly — kings had taken counsel from bishops and magnates for centuries — but the third group in the room: elected representatives of the cities and towns, sitting with the other two and consenting to what was decided. The decrees that came out of it, the Decreta, bound the king to specific undertakings: to keep the peace, to respect the inviolability of the home, to guarantee that no man would be harmed in person or property without a judgement of the courts, and to take counsel with the assembly before making war or peace.

It is worth being exact about what this was and what it was not. It was a curia regia — a royal council — widened by a king who needed the towns’ money and militias, at a moment when his title was under challenge. It was not a standing institution with fixed powers, it did not meet on a regular schedule, and the admission of townsmen did not immediately become a settled right; assemblies of this shape stayed exceptional for decades afterwards. Nor is the surviving text a single clean document: the decreta attributed to 1188 do not form a unified whole, and scholars have shown that some of the provisions were expanded or reworked later, which means the 1188 assembly cannot be read straight off the parchment as it now stands.

With those qualifications made, the claim still stands up. In 2013 UNESCO entered the Decreta of León in its Memory of the World register under the title "The Decreta of León of 1188 - The oldest documentary manifestation of the European parliamentary system", on the ground that here "the institutional presence of the common people in higher-level decision making, together with the king, the church and the nobility, occurs for the first time through the elected representatives of the towns and cities". The claim is documentary, not evolutionary: it says this is the earliest such assembly for which the written record survives, not that every later parliament descends from it. Rival candidates are argued for — the Icelandic Althing is far older as an assembly, the Sicilian parliament of the 1130s is often cited — but neither produces a text showing elected townsmen consenting with king, church and nobility. England’s parliament admitted burgesses in 1265, seventy-seven years later.

contentSections.title: Two marriages and two annulments
paragraphs: In 1191 Alfonso married his first cousin Teresa, a daughter of King Sancho I of Portugal. The relationship was within the prohibited degrees, and Cardinal Gregory pronounced the marriage null in 1195 or 1196. It had produced three children, Sancha, Fernando and Dulce, whose legitimacy and claims would matter a great deal thirty-five years later.

In December 1197 he married again, this time to Berengaria, the eldest daughter of Alfonso VIII of Castile — a match designed to end the feud with Castile and therefore just as objectionable to Rome, since they were first cousins once removed. Innocent III declared it invalid in 1198 and placed the kingdom under interdict; the couple stayed together until 1204 and had five children, among them the future Ferdinand III. When they finally separated, Berengaria returned to Castile with the children.

The consequence was a dynasty split across two annulled marriages, with daughters by the first and sons by the second. Alfonso spent his later years trying to secure the succession for his daughters Sancha and Dulce, precisely to keep León out of Castilian hands — which is the clearest evidence of what he thought the union of the crowns would mean for his kingdom.

contentSections.title: The Extremaduran conquests
paragraphs: The last phase of the reign was the most successful. With Almohad power broken after 1212 and its Iberian territories fragmenting, Alfonso pushed the Leonese frontier down through Extremadura — country no king of León had held. Cáceres fell in April 1229 after several earlier attempts had failed. In the spring of 1230 he took Mérida, the old Roman and Visigothic metropolis, and then Badajoz, carrying the kingdom to the Guadiana.

He built as well as conquered. In 1218 he established a studium generale at Salamanca out of the existing cathedral schools — the institution that became the University of Salamanca, confirmed and endowed by his grandson Alfonso X a generation later. He also leaned on the military orders, above all Santiago and Alcántara, to hold and settle what his armies took, which is how thinly populated frontier country was made defensible at all.

contentSections.title: Death and the union of the crowns
paragraphs: In September 1230 Alfonso travelled into Galicia on pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela and died at Villanueva de Sarria on the 23rd or 24th, aged fifty-nine. He had willed León to his daughters by his first marriage, Sancha and Dulce, expressly to keep it from his son Ferdinand III, who had been king of Castile since 1217.

The will did not hold, and the reason was Berengaria. Ferdinand’s mother negotiated directly with the two princesses and with their own mother, and on 11 December 1230 the Concord of Benavente settled it: Sancha and Dulce renounced their claims to the kingdom in exchange for substantial revenues and estates, and Ferdinand III took León. The crowns of León and Castile were joined, and this time they were never divided again.

The irony is exact. The king who had spent forty-two years keeping León out of Castile’s grip lost it within three months of his death, to his own son, through the diplomacy of the wife the church had made him give up.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: León’s claim to be the cradle of European parliamentarism rests on Alfonso IX, and the city has made the most of it since the UNESCO inscription of 2013. The substance of the claim is narrow and real: in 1188 a king in difficulty called townsmen to his council and accepted written limits on his own power in front of them, and the record of it survives. Everything grander that has been built on that — an unbroken line from León to modern democracy — is later enthusiasm, and the assembly itself remained an occasional instrument rather than a standing one.

His other bequests are more concrete. The frontier he pushed to the Guadiana made Extremadura Leonese and then Castilian, and gave Ferdinand III the base from which Córdoba fell in 1236 and Seville in 1248. Salamanca became the intellectual centre of the peninsula. And the kingdom itself ended with him: after 1230 León was a title inside the Crown of Castile, its cortes merged, its lion quartered with the castle, its separate history closed by the son he had tried to disinherit.
